name: Body wraps

lead: Body wraps give a quickly slimmer-looking waist and lower tape measurement, which people use before an event or photo. The inch loss is visible right away.

The torso or limbs are wrapped in bandages, plastic or neoprene, sometimes after mud or lotion, and sometimes with a sauna suit. Heat and compression cause sweating and temporary water loss and may compress tissue. The FDA has stated that wraps cause temporary water loss rather than fat loss and that the fluid is quickly replaced. Proponents also claim toning, skin firming and toxin removal; reference sources cite no clinical studies for those claims.

paras: Users wrap up for a session at a spa or at home, then measure afterward, timing it close to the occasion since the effect fades as they rehydrate. Some combine wraps with lotions or mud treatments.

The FDA warns that rapid, excessive fluid loss can cause severe dehydration and electrolyte imbalance. Tight wraps and heat add further strain, so people with heart or kidney conditions and those who are heat-sensitive generally avoid them.

web.title: Body Wraps to Lose Weight - Healthline

chain: Slimmer measurements for a short time
angle.text: Wraps and sauna suits give a quickly slimmer-looking waist or a lower tape measurement before an event. The inch loss is visible right away; per the FDA, it is water that returns, and fat loss from wraps is not shown.

lead: Body wraps are spa and home treatments in which the torso, waist or limbs are wrapped in bandages, plastic film or neoprene, often after mud, herbal preparations or lotions are applied, and sometimes combined with a PVC sauna suit. People use them to look slimmer and smoother for a short time, for example before an event, because measurements and skin appearance can change after a session.[1][2]

Healthline reports that wraps are marketed for losing inches, dropping weight and tightening loose skin, with most sessions lasting 30 to 90 minutes and the skin rinsed and moisturized afterwards.[2] Spa options described there include heat wraps, slimming wraps with lotions or herbal products, infrared wraps and 'detoxing' wraps, while neoprene wraps are said to raise core temperature and induce sweating.[2]

Proponents also say wraps hydrate and firm skin, relax muscles and help the body 'flush out toxins'.[1] The US Food and Drug Administration, as summarized by Wikipedia, has stated that inches or pounds lost during a wrap come from sweating and are temporary because the fluid is replaced by drinking and eating.[1] Published medical research on 'body wraps' covers other uses such as therapeutic wraps in psychiatry, neonatal care and burn dressings.[3][4]
infobox: Bandages, mud, plastic film, neoprene, PVC sauna suits
FDA warning on wraps for weight reduction[1]

paras: In a typical spa treatment, mud or another preparation is applied to the skin and the area is covered with bandages, sometimes inside a plastic or PVC suit, to induce sweating.[1] Consumer versions include neoprene waist wraps and sauna suits worn during exercise.[2]

Healthline lists several spa formats: heat wraps, slimming wraps applied with lotions or herbal products, infrared wraps and detoxing wraps said to draw toxins from the skin.[2] Sessions typically run 30 to 90 minutes.[2]

Wrap marketers say heat and compression make the body sweat, tighten the look of the skin and reduce measurements, with claims ranging from a few pounds and inches in one session to several dress sizes over repeated treatments.[2] Wikipedia describes proponents as saying wraps slim, tone, hydrate and firm the body and help with sore muscles and joint inflammation.[1]

The FDA position summarized by Wikipedia is that any weight lost is from fluid and is quickly regained, that wraps do not affect fat deposits, and that fat is reduced when calorie intake falls below energy expenditure.[1] Healthline reports that most supporting evidence comes from companies that sell wraps and that little unbiased research exists; it adds that skin may look tighter afterward but often only for a short time.[2]

The FDA warning cited by Wikipedia states that rapid, excessive fluid loss can cause severe dehydration and electrolyte imbalance.[1] Healthline lists dehydration, overheating, discomfort from tight compression and unknown reactions to herbal, exfoliating or moisturizing ingredients as risks.[2]
The sources Wikipedia cites for the FDA warning are a 1982 FDA Consumer article and a 2009 ABC News report.[1]

No studies found on cosmetic slimming wraps. Medical literature on 'body wraps' concerns other uses: a randomized feasibility trial of therapeutic wet and dry sheet wraps in children with autism and severe injurious behaviour, observational work on therapeutic wraps in healthy volunteers and psychiatric wards, neonatal skin-to-skin wraps, and plastic wraps for heat retention during surgery.[3][4][5][6]

lore.intro: Wraps are promoted by spas and wrap brands and covered by health media, mostly for short-term inch loss before events.[2]

claims.claim: Wraps shrink inches in a single session

timeline.event: An FDA Consumer article by Judith Willis warns against body wraps as a weight-reduction method.[1]
ABC News reports on risks of body wraps.[1]
Healthline publishes a medically reviewed explainer on body wraps for weight loss.[2]
